transcript: Meeting header: 2026-08-20 15:00 PDT | Duration: 48 min | Attendees: Maya Chen, Liam O'Connor (Redwood) — Aisha Patel, Marco Silva, Dora Nguyen (ZenOps)

Summary: quick check-in on the BurstBench runs; discuss tuning knobs — continuous batching, concurrency caps, queue shaping/backpressure — and decide next benchmark steps. Short security ask review and handoff items.
Topics: 1) Latest burstbench results 2) Queueing behavior and p99 spikes 3) Concurrency targets and batching gains 4) Next benchmark & artifacts to share
00:00 Maya: okay everyone thanks for jumping on, we'll keep this to about 45 minutes, quick recap of last week's run — Liam do you want to take us through the numbers?

00:12 Liam: yep, so run-2 we saw steady state throughput at ~420 rps for the 2K token prompt mix, batch size averaged 18, tokens/sec moved from 9.8k to about 24k once KV cache warmed up, p95 was healthy but p99 had these microspikes around 480-520ms, which corresponded to queue depth surges — looks like backpressure from our downstream batching window kicks in when concurrency crosses 10
01:05 Aisha: sorry can I interrupt, when you say concurrency crosses 10 that is per-gpu concurrency? how do you define that relative to our container count and autoscale policy?

01:20 Liam: good call — it's per-worker concurrency target, our test used 4 workers on the instance type and a target concurrency of 12 total, so effectively 3 per worker. In practice with your deployment you'd map workers to pods, but the important bit is how many inflight requests go to the model runner before we form a batch

02:08 Marco: the p99 spikes mean for our user flows — some of our endpoints are latency-sensitive. we can tolerate some tail, but not consistent 500ms blips. were those correlated to cold KV cache misses?

02:22 Liam: partly yes — first 30 seconds after a scale up K V cache misses cause extra processing; but we also saw spikes that aligned with burst arrivals where queueing latency increased and the batching window waited up to 120ms to assemble a larger batch — tradeoff is throughput vs latency. we can lower the wait threshold to reduce spikes but you'll lose tokens/sec efficiency
03:10 Dora: can you translate that into cost — like how much does lowering batching wait add to token compute cost?

03:25 Maya: rough numbers — in this profile reducing batch window from 120ms to 40ms dropped batch size from 18 to 9 and increased cost per token by ~18% in our run estimates. we'll produce a short cost delta spreadsheet, but it's a tradeoff you should decide based on SLOs
04:05 Aisha: we are leaning towards tighter latency for checkout flows, but for background enrichment we can accept higher latencies. can Redwood route requests by class?

04:20 Liam: yes, smart routing is straightforward — you can tag routes so latency-sensitive endpoints hit a low-latency pool (dedicated) or use a lower batching target; lower throughput but guaranteed tail. For the POC we recommended mixed routing during the benchmark — route 20% traffic to low-latency config and 80% to throughput-optimized config

05:00 Marco: on scaling, we noticed that when queue depth hit around 180 the autoscaler added nodes but the newly warm nodes took time which caused additional queuing. is there a burst capacity or graceful fallback pattern we can use?

05:20 Liam: yes, there's a burst capacity policy — you can allocate a small reserved burst pool to handle sudden arrivals, and also fallback to a smaller model variant during spikes. For this POC we tried fallback disabled, maybe next run we enable a 2-instance warm standby

06:05 Maya: quick security check — Marco asked last week about KMS and audit logs. We uploaded the SOC2 summary; I'll share the direct link after the call. Also Redwood can support customer-managed KMS for Private deployments.
06:40 Marco: great. small note: the transcription earlier said "K V cache" with spaces in the doc — just FYI, that's our internal term too sometimes, so no worries

07:02 Liam: thanks. next, on the technical side we tried enabling continuous batching in run-2 which reduces batching latency variance by draining small idle batches more aggressively. The metric we liked: variance in batch size dropped by 48% and median latency improved by ~22ms, but the p99 still had those outliers tied to queue saturation
08:10 Aisha: when you say continuous batching drains small idle batches, do you mean it will send smaller batches earlier? that seems to undermine throughput

08:25 Liam: it sends them sooner but uses a dynamic micro-window to not kill batching efficiency. think of it as a soft-cap that lets the runtime finish a batch early if it has been waiting beyond threshold. we tune that threshold depending on your latency SLOs
09:00 Dora: can you show an example config you used? like concurrency X, batch window Y, queue size Z?

09:12 Liam: sure — run-2 config snippet: concurrency_target=12, batch_max=32, batch_wait_ms=120, continuous_batching=true, kv_cache_warmup=30s, queue_max_depth=250. I'll paste the exact run config in the slack thread after the call

10:05 Maya: we saw in the logs that a small percentage of requests had downstream tokenization overhead — those were the ones causing longer tail. We'll send a note on recommended client-side tokenization and header trimming best practices
11:00 Marco: curious about real-world mapping — in prod we expect 800 rps sustained with 2k token avg, plus daily bursts. are you confident the current config will scale linearly?

11:18 Liam: with current instance type and quantization profile we projected linear scaling up to about 1.6k rps before you need additional replicas; the biggest limiter will be KV cache cold starts on new replicas and network egress if you have large payloads. For predictable scaling, Reserved/Dedicated or pre-warmed standbys help
12:10 Aisha: ok specific ask — can we run another burstbench with concurrency targets set to 8/12/16 and continuous batching toggled off/on to see delta?
12:25 Liam: yes that's exactly plan for burstbench-3. we'll capture container metrics, kernel stalls, and queue depth histograms
13:00 Dora: also include a run with a small model fallback at 50% threshold so we can see quality vs cost tradeoffs
13:10 Liam: noted — fallback to smaller quantized variant at 50% queue threshold will be included as an experimental run
14:00 Marco: can you also include the p99 breakdown by internal vs external queueing latency? we saw some of the time is queuing inside the runtime vs waiting for batch formation
14:16 Liam: yes we'll split p99 into run-queue, batch-wait, compute and kv-miss components, that will help pinpoint bottlenecks
15:20 Maya: quick commercial note — if you plan dedicated, there are commit tiers that change unit pricing substantially; I'll send an apples-to-apples with the POC numbers
16:05 Aisha: on security — does Redwood capture per-request audit logs and allow retention levels? we have compliance needs for 180 days retention and redaction options

16:25 Maya: yes, audit logs available and retention configurable as an add-on. We provide redaction filters and can integrate with your SIEM; I'll include the SOC2 appendix and the audit log documentation link
17:12 Marco: small question about telemetry — the dashboard we saw had tokens/sec but not a clear cost breakdown per route. can you add token-level cost by route?
17:30 Liam: yep we'll add per-route token cost and p99 latency overlays in the next dashboard snapshot. That will help you decide which endpoints to route to low-latency pools
18:10 Aisha: during last run we had an anomaly at 29:12 where a spike correlated with an infra noise — do you have logs for that timestamp?

18:22 Liam: yes that's in the run-2 logs — looks like a kernel scheduling stall on the host, maybe noisy neighbor on the cloud instance. We'll mark that and exclude from steady-state stats but include as note
19:00 Dora: what about on-prem options? some of our customers require VPC or fully air-gapped packages — would performance profile change?
19:18 Maya: performance is similar with private deployments but you may lose some autoscaling flexibility; also network topology affects KV cache warmup. We'll outline expectations in the runbook
20:05 Marco: question on telemetry retention cost — storing high-res container metrics for 30 days is expensive; can you downsample?
20:20 Liam: yes we can provide high-res for 48 hours then 1-minute aggregated for 30 days. We'll include a telemetry retention recommendation
21:10 Aisha: once you run burstbench-3, what artifact will you share?
21:20 Liam: deliverables: tarball of run logs, metrics CSVs, dashboard link, config snippets, and an executive one-pager with recommended concurrency and batch settings for ZenOps traffic

22:05 Maya: next steps recap — Liam runs burstbench-3; Maya shares SOC2 and pricing; ZenOps provides traffic sample. then we'll meet after the run to decide pilot ramp. tentative follow-up 60-min on 2026-08-27 at same time
23:00 Aisha: sounds good. small nit — some of the variable names in the dashboard use internal shorthand like "cbatch" — could you make them more explicit for our execs?
23:12 Liam: good point, we'll expand labels and include a legend in the dashboard
24:00 Marco: one more ops ask — can we get a short runbook describing how to flip fallback and burst pool on/off? engineers should be able to toggle without a full deploy
24:15 Maya: yes we have a playbook; I'll add an operations checklist for toggles and include access controls required
25:05 Dora: given the numbers so far, I'm cautiously optimistic. If the next run shows stable p99 under the low-latency config we can move to a limited pilot with customers in two weeks
25:30 Maya: great. anything else urgent?
25:40 Speaker 1: quick question about tokenization overhead — are you recommending client-side or server-side tokenization for lowest latency?

26:00 Liam: client-side tokenization generally reduces server work and network bytes. For fairness in benchmarks we used server-side to match your current prod. If you can shift critical endpoints to client-side, you'll shave a small but helpful amount off p50/p90 latencies
27:00 Aisha: ok we'll try a client-side tokenization prototype against the staging bench
28:05 Liam: small note — we saw some log noise from container restarts at 12:34 in the run; that's an instrumentation bug on our end, we fixed it in the runtime build to be used in burstbench-3
29:00 Marco: excellent. do you have a recommended concurrency ceiling per GPU?

29:12 Liam: it depends on model size and quantization, but for your 7B-ish variant we saw best results at 3-4 concurrency per worker on this instance type. pushing beyond that increases batch formation latency and p99 instability
30:00 Dora: any major risks we should call out?

30:12 Liam: main risks — KV cache cold starts on scale-up, noisy neighbor stalls on shared infra, and misconfigured batching windows. Mitigations: pre-warmed standbys, reserved burst pool, and conservative batch_wait_ms defaults
31:00 Maya: we'll compile these into the risk section of the one-pager

32:00 Aisha: ok let's lock the due dates then. Marco will share traffic sample by 8/22, Liam will run burstbench-3 and share by 8/24, Maya will share SOC2 link and pricing by 8/21. meeting on 8/27 to review
33:00 Marco: agreed. thanks everyone
33:10 Maya: thanks all — we'll follow up in the thread with configs and links

33:30 End of meeting notes: total recorded time 48 minutes. Some filler and minor cross-talk present in transcript. References shared: link to run-2 dashboard (internal), SOC2 summary (link to doc), sample pricing spreadsheet (will be attached).
